statement: Trade terminology or usage evidence may be admitted to explain the trade meaning of a contract term. The reason is the trade-meaning function, not an express agreement by the parties.
trigger: A contract phrase is explained by someone familiar with the relevant wholesale trade.

statement: Opinion form alone does not exclude qualified specialized-knowledge testimony.
trigger: An answer says to exclude testimony simply because it is an opinion.

statement: On an admissibility call, first name what the testimony is offered to prove. Pick the answer that labels that use, not the answer that repeats a tempting background fact.
trigger: Three choices say admitted, but for different reasons.

statement: Marital communications privilege protects a confidential communication between spouses during marriage; the communication can be written or electronic, not only spoken.
trigger: private written message between spouses during marriage
authority: FRE 501; SEC v. Lavin; Wolfle v. United States; Trammel v. United States

statement: When privilege answers fight over spoken words, document format, and refusal to testify, ask what object the privilege protects.
trigger: one answer says document; one says spoken; one says spouse refuses

statement: Spousal testimonial privilege and confidential marital communications privilege are separate. Testimonial privilege requires a current marriage; communications privilege can protect confidential private communications made during the marriage even after divorce.
trigger: Divorced former spouse + private statement made during marriage.
authority: FRE 501; Trammel v. United States; Pereira v. United States.

statement: When the answer set splits sustain/overrule and testimonial/communications, pick the route that matches the timing facts: divorced now, private communication then.
trigger: Two sustain answers with different privilege labels.

statement: For hearsay within hearsay, each layer needs its own path. In an employee-transcript item, check the employee statement layer and the transcript/public-record layer separately.
trigger: Transcript of earlier testimony offered for its truth.

statement: Former testimony needs the current opponent, or a civil predecessor, to have had an opportunity and similar motive to develop the earlier testimony.
trigger: Earlier criminal trial; later civil defendant was not a party.

statement: When a choice says 'transcript,' split the evidence into speaker layer and document layer before choosing an exception.
trigger: Transcript offered in a later trial.

statement: Crime-fraud is purpose-based, not topic-based: privilege fails only when legal advice is sought to commit, continue, or cover up crime or fraud.
trigger: Client asks whether planned conduct would be fraudulent and says she will not do it if unlawful.
authority: FRE 501 common law; United States v. Zolin; Clark v. United States.

statement: Substantial need is a work-product concept; it is not the test for overriding attorney-client communications.
trigger: A privilege answer says 'substantial need.'
authority: Federal privilege and work-product doctrine distinction.

statement: When a privilege answer says 'fraud,' do not stop at the topic. Name the axis: compliance advice versus using the lawyer to further fraud.
trigger: Client says she will not proceed if the conduct is fraudulent.

statement: Relevant evidence does not need to prove the whole case by itself. If it has any tendency to make a consequential fact more probable, it clears the relevance threshold.
trigger: The opponent says the evidence could have another explanation.
authority: Fed. R. Evid. 401, 402, 403; see pass-1 legal verification.

statement: In a relevance array, cut 'conclusive,' 'always,' and 'only' before weighing the story. The survivor usually states what the evidence tends to show.
trigger: Three choices narrow admissibility; one states the fact relation.

statement: Rule 610 blocks religion-as-truthfulness evidence. It does not block religious affiliation or organizational ties when offered to show bias, interest, or relationship to a party.
trigger: religion objection plus paid role or organizational tie to a party
authority: Federal Rule of Evidence 610 Advisory Committee Note

statement: When an Evidence answer turns on the same fact being used for different credibility purposes, name the offered purpose first and grade only that lane.
trigger: The stem says 'offered to show bias' and 'not to show truthfulness.'

statement: A physical object does not reach the jury on 'maybe.' The proponent must first supply some link supporting a finding that the object is what it claims or is connected to the case.
trigger: An object is offered, but the stem gives no identifying witness, no marks, and no source facts.

statement: When a choice says the jury can weigh it, first ask whether the item crossed the foundation gate. No gate, no weight.
trigger: The proponent says the jury can decide what to make of an unidentified object.

statement: Rule 407 is not negligence-only: it bars later fixes offered to prove product defect, design defect, or a need for warning or instruction. Feasibility is only a separate permitted purpose when it is genuinely disputed and actually offered for that purpose.
trigger: Post-injury redesign or stronger warning offered in a product case.
authority: Federal Rule of Evidence 407; 1997 Advisory Committee note.

statement: When the stem tells you why evidence is offered, hold that purpose fixed. Relevance and exception words do not matter until they match the stated purpose.
trigger: The stem says the later measure is offered to prove defect or inadequate warning.

statement: In Evidence, start with the bridge: what fact does this item help prove in this case? If the stem gives no bridge, do not jump to object category, demonstrative use, or prejudice.
trigger: A physical object is offered, but the stem says no witness connects it to the defendant, document, event, or issue.
